newsitem.title: CANADA: Union says no way to avoid GM Canada strike.
newsitem.headline: Union says no way to avoid GM Canada strike.

text.p: As the clock winds down to a midnight strike deadline, Canadian Auto Workers union President Buzz Hargrove said on Wednesday there was "absolutely no way" to avoid a strike at General Motors Corp.'s Canadian unit.
Hargrove said he felt there was not enough time to bridge what appeared to be a widening gap on several issues ahead of the 11:59 p.m. EDT (3:59 a.m. GMT Thursday) deadline.

"I would say there is absolutely no way possible we can avoid a shutdown of the Oshawa (Ontario) operations and the Ste-Therese (Quebec) operations as of 11:59 (EDT) tonight," Hargrove told a news briefing.
Analysts said a strike at all of GM's Canadian operations could cost the parent company up to $150 million a week in lost profits and squeeze vehicle inventories in as little as one week.
Hargrove said it might be difficult to keep talks with GM going once an escalating strike began.

"The question will be can we keep the discussions going in a productive manner and start to deal with some of the issues and recognise that General Motors has no right to argue that it cannot meet the standards," Hargrove added.
Earlier this week, the union approved an escalating strike strategy in which 15,500 of its 28,000 GM members would go on strike at midnight on Wednesday.
Other GM Canada facilities would join the strike starting on Oct. 6 and the entire Canadian operation would be shut down by Oct. 9.

GM could lose between $50 million to $60 million a week from the shutdown of assembly operations alone, said David Healy, an analyst at Burnham Securities Inc. A full-fledged work stoppage could take $150 million a week out of profits, he said.

Although it has some important parts plants, Healy said a strike at all of GM's Canadian operations would not bring the world's largest automaker to its knees, like the 17-day work stoppage at two Dayton, Ohio, brake plants in March did. That strike cost GM $900 million.

GM Canada spokesman Stew Low said the company was hopeful a strike could still be avoided if the union moved from its determination to apply the exact pattern of the deal it forged with Chrysler Corp.'s Canadian unit slightly more than a week ago.
"All we're asking for is some flexibility in order to fit some of the pattern issues to where we need to take our business," he said.
The CAW traditionally picks an initial strike target and sets a pattern agreement that it applies to the other two North American auto companies.
Hargrove said the union hoped for a short strike, but said it could last longer.

The CAW has said its C$50 million ($36.5 million) strike fund could last up to eight weeks. That could stretch to 16 weeks if the union mortgaged some properties. Hargrove has also said that the union set a special strike dues convention for Oct. 18 for the entire 210,000 membership of the CAW.
The major unresolved issue in the talks is the contracting out of jobs to non-union suppliers, generally known as "outsourcing".
GM Canada said it planned to sell two Ontario plants and outsource work at several plants for a total cost of 5,500 CAW jobs and the union has said it is determined to resist.
But the company and the union said many other sticking points remained in the talks. With only 10 hours left until workers hit the picket lines, GM had not delivered a promised economic package.
GM Canada's Low said that in addition to outsourcing, the carmaker needed flexibility from the union on a host of work time and work rule issues.

"We understand the pattern on economic issues, but he's expanded that to a number of other legislative areas like work standards and all kinds of other things that just don't fit with where we need to be," Low said.
